summary.en: An invariant explains completed work at every step.
summary.bn: লুপ দিয়ে গুণফল, মৌলিক সংখ্যা, গসাগু ও অঙ্কের পরিচিত সমস্যাগুলো ধাপে ধাপে সমাধান করো।

notes: The algorithms use C17 and long long from C99. No example depends on integer overflow or a floating approximation to an exact digit power. The chosen input bounds are part of the correctness argument.

examples.title: Factorial with its zero case
examples.explanationHtml: Starting from one, the product becomes two, six, twenty-four and one hundred twenty. No multiplication is needed for n zero or one, so the same initialization gives the correct empty product. The input bound twenty prevents unsigned long long overflow.

examples.title: A Fibonacci pair
examples.explanationHtml: The pair starts at zero and one. Each printed a is followed by a simultaneous-style pair advance using a saved next value. The eight terms end at thirteen. The bound used in the exercises keeps even the extra computed next term inside unsigned long long.

examples.title: Prime check with a division bound
examples.explanationHtml: Twenty-nine survives candidate divisors two through five. Six would exceed the positive square-root bound expressed by n/d, so no further divisor is needed. Starting prime from n >= 2 rejects zero and one before the loop can wrongly accept them.

examples.title: Primes in a small range
examples.explanationHtml: The outer loop tests each candidate from one through fifteen. The inner loop rejects composite values, while one is excluded by definition. The resulting primes are separated by one space. A found flag also lets the program name an empty result explicitly.

examples.title: Euclid GCD and a safe LCM product
examples.explanationHtml: The pair changes from forty-eight/eighteen to eighteen/twelve, twelve/six and six/zero. The GCD is six. Dividing forty-eight by six before multiplying by eighteen gives LCM one hundred forty-four. The widened product avoids an unnecessary int intermediate.

examples.title: A palindrome keeps its original
examples.explanationHtml: The reversal takes the digits from the right and builds another integer. The saved original stays 1221 while n becomes zero. Comparing the reversed result with that original gives one. The do-while also handles zero as a valid one-digit case.

examples.title: Armstrong uses the actual digit count
examples.explanationHtml: The first digit pass counts four positions. Each digit is then multiplied into an integer power four times. The fourth-power sum equals 1634, so the output is one. A fixed cube would give the wrong answer for this four-digit candidate.

examples.title: A perfect-number divisor sum
examples.explanationHtml: The loop checks divisors through three and adds one, two and three. Their sum equals six, so the predicate is true. The extra n > 1 guard excludes one, whose empty proper-divisor sum cannot make it perfect.

practice.title: A bounded factorial
practice.statementHtml: Read n 0 to 20. After the prompt Input: , print n factorial as unsigned long long and newline.

practice.title: First Fibonacci terms
practice.statementHtml: Read n 0 to 60. After the prompt Input: , print the first n Fibonacci terms starting 0,1, with single spaces and a final newline. For zero, print only the newline.
hints: Compute next before replacing the pair.

practice.title: A bounded prime interval
practice.statementHtml: Read low and high with 0 <= low <= high <= 1000. After the prompt Input: , print primes in the closed interval with single spaces, or None if empty; finish with newline.
hints: Each candidate needs its own primality flag.

practice.title: GCD and LCM with zero
practice.statementHtml: Read a and b 0 to 1000000. After the prompt Input: , print their GCD and LCM separated by a space and newline. Define GCD(0,0)=0 and LCM=0 if either input is zero.
hints: Do not divide by a zero GCD.

practice.title: General decimal Armstrong check
practice.statementHtml: Read n 0 to 999999. After the prompt Input: , print 1 when n equals the sum of its digits raised to its digit count, otherwise 0; end with newline.
hints: Use a do-while digit count and integer powers.

quiz.prompt: What initial product makes zero factorial correct?
quiz.explanation: The product of no factors is one.

quiz.prompt: Why save the next Fibonacci value before replacing a?
options: Both old pair values are needed
quiz.explanation: Overwriting one too early loses part of the sum.

quiz.prompt: Why can primality testing stop at the square root?
options: Every prime is smaller than its root
A nontrivial factor pair has a member at most that bound
quiz.explanation: If neither factor were small, their product would exceed n.

quiz.prompt: What quantity stays the same in Euclid replacement?
quiz.explanation: Replacing a by its remainder preserves common divisibility.

quiz.prompt: Why divide before multiplying in LCM?
options: It reduces the intermediate product size
It makes zero GCD safe automatically
quiz.explanation: The equivalent formula is safer when the GCD is nonzero.

quiz.prompt: Which power belongs in an Armstrong test?
Which divisors belong in a perfect-number sum?
options: Positive divisors smaller than the number
quiz.explanation: Proper divisors exclude the number being tested.

quiz.prompt: An empty factorial loop starts with one. Which result prints?
quiz.explanation: The product initialization already represents zero factorial.

quiz.prompt: Euclid on 18 and 12 ends with which GCD and LCM?
quiz.explanation: The GCD is six and the divide-first LCM is thirty-six.

quiz.prompt: One has no proper positive divisors. Which perfect flag appears?
quiz.explanation: One is excluded and its divisor sum is zero.

quiz.prompt: For n = 0, how many decimal digits should the Armstrong power use?
quiz.explanation: The decimal representation of zero has one digit.

quiz.prompt: Why is the primality bound d <= n / d useful for positive n?
options: It avoids a potentially overflowing d*d product
quiz.explanation: The division expresses the square-root bound without forming the square.

quiz.prompt: Which proper divisors make six perfect?
quiz.explanation: Proper divisors exclude the number itself; one plus two plus three equals six.

examQuestions.question: Read n 0 to 999999. After Input: print 1 when n equals the sum of its digits raised to its digit count, otherwise 0; end with newline.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int n;
    printf("Input: ");
    if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 0 || n > 999999) {
        return 1;
    }
    int original = n;
    int copy = n;
    int digits = 0;
    do {
        digits++;
        copy /= 10;
    } while (copy > 0);
    int sum = 0;
    do {
        int digit = n % 10;
        int power = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < digits; i++) {
            power *= digit;
        }
        sum += power;
        n /= 10;
    } while (n > 0);
    printf("%d\n", sum == original);
    return 0;
}

Use a do-while digit count and integer powers.
